Reading · work and interviews

1.1 Discuss. Have you ever had a job interview? What is the most difficult question you have been asked — or can imagine being asked?

KEY WORDS

a candidate a person applying for a job

qualifications your certificates and training

likeable pleasant, easy to get on with

turn down to refuse or reject

Not the Best Interview I've Ever Had

Bahodir has been working in recruitment for eleven years, and he says he has stopped being surprised. “I've interviewed maybe three thousand people,” he told me. “I've had a candidate answer his phone in the middle of my question. I've had someone bring his mother. Last spring a woman arrived forty minutes late, sat down, and said, quite calmly, that the traffic was my fault for choosing an office in the city centre.”

What interests him more than the disasters, though, is a quieter pattern. Over the years he has noticed that the candidates who get hired are frequently not the ones with the strongest qualifications. “I've turned down brilliant people,” he admits, “and I've hired people who looked ordinary on paper. The difference is almost always the same thing: can I imagine sitting next to this person for eight hours?”

Research supports him. Studies of hiring decisions have repeatedly found that likeability predicts job offers better than technical skill does, particularly in roles that involve working in teams. This is uncomfortable — it sounds unfair, and sometimes it is. But there is a defence: skills can be taught in a few months, whereas a difficult colleague remains a difficult colleague for years.

Bahodir's advice for candidates is refreshingly practical. Prepare two or three real examples of things you have actually done, not adjectives about yourself. Ask a genuine question about the team. And if the interview goes badly, remember that it usually says less about you than you fear. “I turned down someone in 2019 who now runs a company twice the size of ours,” he said. “I think about that man more than he thinks about me.”

2

Grammar · present perfect and past simple

PRESENTATION

PRESENT PERFECT — the time is unfinished, unknown or unimportant:

I have interviewed three thousand people. · She has worked here for years.

PAST SIMPLE — the time is finished and stated or understood:

I interviewed her last spring. · He left the company in 2019.

Present perfect

Past simple

ever, never, just, already, yet, so far

yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago, then

I've had three jobs.

I had my first job in 2015.

She's worked here for ten years.

She worked there for ten years.

Have you ever been to a job fair?

Did you go to the fair last month?

ERROR WARNING

A finished time expression forces the past simple:

I have started this job last year. ✗ I started this job last year. ✓

for + a period · since + a starting point:

I've worked here for six years. · I've worked here since 2020.

been = went and came back · gone = still away: She's been to Paris · She's gone to Paris.

Everyday English · making and responding to suggestions

4.1 Read the conversation.

Nodira I've had three interviews this month and no offers. I don't know what I'm doing wrong.

Aziz Why don't you ask for feedback? Most companies will tell you.

Nodira That's a good idea, actually. I've never thought of that.

Aziz You could also practise with someone before the real thing.

Nodira Hmm, I'm not sure. It feels a bit artificial.

Aziz How about recording yourself instead?

Nodira Now that I like. I'll try it this week.

5

Writing · an email giving news

5.1 Write an email (120–150 words) to a friend telling them you have started a new job.

PLAN

Opening — greet and say why you're writing. Body — the news (present perfect), then details (past simple). Closing — a question and a friendly ending.

Useful language: Guess what! · I've just… · It happened like this… · Anyway, how are you? · Write soon!
